title: Hazel and Corvus Find the Moon-Bunny
markdown:
The moon climbed high, painting the Tall Mountains with silver light. In a little cottage nestled among the softest green moss and the nicest pine trees lived a young witch named Hazel. She loved the warm smell of lavender tea brewing in her kettle and the happy shine of her broomstick, which she polished until it sparkled like a dragonfly’s wing. She was not a witch who made loud potions that went poof, or cast spiky spells that made things go zap. Hazel’s magic was the gentle kind. It made flowers grow a little brighter. It helped lost ladybugs find their way home to their leaf. It made sleepy bees wake up with a cheerful buzz.

Her constant friend, always by her side, was Corvus. Corvus was a crow, and his feathers shone like shiny black stones, catching the moonlight so that he looked like a little piece of the night sky had come to visit. He had a beak for talking and a mind full of questions.

“Hazel, Hazel,” he would caw, his voice like small stones rattling in a box. “Did you see that cloud up there? It looked exactly like a sleepy badger taking a nap. Or perhaps it looked like a giant teacup, ready for a sip of cloud-juice.”

Hazel would smile, a warm wrinkled smile that made her bright curious eyes crinkle. “Indeed, Corvus. It does look like a teacup. And a very nice one at that, fit for a giant bear.”

This evening Hazel was tidying her little herb garden, humming a soft happy tune that floated on the air like a dandelion puff. The air was growing cooler, carrying damp earth after a warm day and the fresh clean smell of pine needles.

Suddenly Corvus, perched on the garden fence, let out a series of very excited caws. “Hazel! Hazel! Look! Down there, by the Whispering Pines! There’s something small and all alone!”

Hazel followed his sharp gaze. Near the edge of the rustling pine forest sat a tiny ball of fluff. It looked a little like a baby rabbit, but its fur was the softest palest colour, like moonlight gathered in a cloud. Its long thin ears bent down with a gentle sadness. It was a moon-bunny, a creature rarely seen so far from its cozy home. This little one was plainly lost. A tiny flutter, not of cold but of worry, went through Hazel’s heart.

“Oh, the poor thing,” Hazel whispered. “It’s all alone. And the night will be here very soon. It will be so dark.”

Corvus hopped from one foot to the other on the fence, his little head bobbing. “But where does it belong, Hazel? Does it have a mama? Or a papa? Perhaps it likes to play hide-and-seek and just forgot where to hide. Hide-and-seek is such fun!”

The sun was sinking fast, painting the sky in deeper orange and purple. The moon was just beginning to peek over the tallest peak, like a shy silver button.

“We can’t leave it here all by itself, Corvus,” Hazel said, firm but kind. “We simply must help it find its home. It’s getting very late for such a little creature to be on its own.”

She gathered a few things from her cottage. First, a small woven basket lined with the softest moss she had collected, like a tiny comfy bed. Then a small pouch filled with glowing moon-petals. These were not for big noisy spells. They were for gentle soft light, like tiny winking stars, to guide their way through the darkening woods.

“Come, Corvus. We’ll find its family together.”

Hazel, with the little moon-bunny nestled safely in her moss-lined basket, and Corvus fluttering a little ahead like a black-feathered scout, stepped toward the whispering pines.

The soft pine needles made a lovely gentle crunch under Hazel’s worn boots. Corvus darted from branch to branch.

“This way, Hazel! Or perhaps that way! Oh, wait, I think it was the other way! So many trees, so many directions! My beak is getting tired from all this pointing!”

Hazel smiled at his cheerful chatter, which made the darkening woods feel much less vast. She opened her pouch, and the moon-petals opened up, casting a soft silvery glow that danced on the rough bark of the trees.

They walked for a little while, the gentle light showing them the winding path. The moon-bunny twitched its long ears, but still looked a little sad and very small in the basket. Then, from the deep shadows of a large moss-covered rock that looked like a sleeping giant, stepped a figure as old as the mountains themselves. It was Elder Elara, an elf whose robe seemed woven from the softest forest moss and the shimmering morning mist. Her eyes twinkled like distant stars. Her smile was as gentle as a summer breeze.

“Good evening, young witch and your feathered friend,” Elder Elara said, her voice like the rustle of autumn leaves. “And what brings you so deep into the woods at this twilight hour?”

Hazel explained all about the lost moon-bunny. Elder Elara nodded slowly.

“Ah, yes. This little one belongs to the Moon-Bunny Warren, high up on the Stony Ridge. They will be very worried, I am sure. But the path can be tricky in the twilight, especially if you don’t know the way.” She pointed a long slender finger that seemed to glow faintly. “Follow this deer trail, and it will lead you to the base of the ridge. Then look for the twin sparkling ferns. That’s where the hidden path begins.”

Hazel felt a spark of hope flutter in her chest, like a butterfly. “Thank you, Elder Elara.”

Corvus cawed, flapping his wings. “Twin sparkling ferns! Not just one, but two! Imagine that!”

The path Elder Elara had shown them was quite clear. Soon they reached a place where the trees thinned, revealing a tall rocky hill that led upwards. The moon was higher now, a bright friendly circle, casting long soft shadows on the rocks.

“Look, Hazel!” Corvus chirped. His keen eyes had spotted the ferns nestled beside a big rock. They sparkled with a faint silver light, just as Elder Elara had said, almost as if they were whispering secrets to the moon. They stood in a small quiet clearing.

Hazel looked around. There were no burrows to be seen, no signs of a warren. The moon-bunny in her basket let out a soft tiny whimper.

“Oh, Corvus,” she whispered. “Where could they be? We’re here, but we can’t see their home anywhere.”

Corvus, for once, was quiet, looking around with his bright beady eyes. The moon-bunny nestled closer into the soft moss, its little nose twitching. The moonlight felt cool on Hazel’s cheek. The pine needles under her feet felt prickly.

They did not rush the next look. Hazel sat on a low stone and let the moon-petals rest in her open palm. One fern uncurled a little further, as if it too were waiting. Corvus washed a wing. The bunny’s ears stayed down.

Then a soft rustling came from behind the large boulder. Elder Elara stepped gracefully into the moonlight once more.

“Patience, little witch,” she said, with a gentle smile. “The path is often hidden from plain sight, and sometimes you just need a little help to see it.”

She tapped the base of the large boulder with her staff. With a soft low rumble, a small opening appeared in the rock, almost invisible until now, like a secret doorway.

“They are inside,” Elder Elara whispered. “They heard your approach and knew you were bringing their little one home.”

A chorus of soft happy squeaks emerged from the opening, a sound like tiny bells. The moon-bunny in Hazel’s basket wiggled with excitement, its long ears perked up.

Hazel carefully set the basket down on the soft mossy ground. The mother moon-bunny, with fur as white and soft as the moon itself, hopped out and nudged her lost little one with the sweetest most tender little nudges. There were happy squeaks and gentle nudges all around. Hazel felt a warmth spread through her chest, even warmer than her favorite mug of lavender tea.

Corvus let out a satisfied caw, his tail feathers fanned out proudly. “Well done, Hazel! We found them! And I only got lost… well, only a little bit! And that was very important pointing work!”

Elder Elara’s eyes twinkled. She did not add a speech. She only watched the warren settle, then lifted her staff in a small goodbye.

With a final happy squeak from the grateful moon-bunny family, Hazel and Corvus turned back toward home. The moon was high and bright now, a friendly glowing lantern in the vast velvet sky. The path back felt shorter. As they stepped into their cozy little cottage, Hazel felt tired, her eyelids drooping just a little. She pulled her covers up warm in her bed. Corvus settled on his favorite spot nearby. Outside, the pines kept their quiet. The moon-petals in the pouch had gone dim, their work already done.
characters: Hazel (young witch of the Tall Mountains), Corvus (chatty night-black crow)
